workload: Indemnity claims adjudication runs as several dependent stages: pull the claim data off the submitted documents, validate it against the group certificate in force on the date of service, cross-check the diagnosis codes against the member's own claim history, then route anything flagged to a reviewer. The certificate that governs a claim is itself the hard part — the version in the system may have been superseded by a change request that was never applied. A run that dies halfway through must not redo the stages that already completed, and every figure a reviewer sees has to trace back to the document it came from.

Adjudicating one indemnity claim means four things in sequence and we currently do them by hand. Read the submitted paperwork. Check it against whichever version of the group certificate was live on the treatment date — and the system's copy is not always the live one, because change requests get raised and never applied. Compare the diagnosis codes with what that member has claimed before. Send anything odd to a reviewer, who will want to see where each number came from. These take a while and we cannot afford to start over when one falls over midway.

Total-loss motor claims move through four sub-processes end to end: intake of the adjuster paperwork and valuation reports, a settlement calculation, a lienholder and title check, and a payout authorisation that a human signs. Each stage produces evidence the next stage depends on, some stages wait on external parties for days, and an exception at any point has to park the file without losing the work already done.

A written-off vehicle claim passes through intake of the adjuster paperwork, a settlement figure, a title and lienholder check, then a human authorising the payout. Each step needs what the step before it produced. Some of them sit waiting on a third party for days. If something goes wrong at step three we want the file parked, not the first two steps thrown away.

Policy binders and freedom-of-service sheets feed our booking systems across three regions and nineteen lines of business. The pipeline orchestrates the whole booking end to end, and the binders themselves are not uniform — the aviation ones list fifteen to twenty aircraft each, which is where our current extraction stops returning everything. Booking cannot complete until the governing schedule for each line is resolved, and part-completed runs have to resume rather than restart.

We book insurance policies from binders and freedom-of-service sheets across nineteen lines of business in three regions. The binders are not uniform — an aviation one can list twenty aircraft, and our current reader stops short of the end on those. Nothing can be booked until we have settled which schedule governs the line, and a run that stops partway needs to pick up where it left off.

Our clinical specialists go through a patient chart, bookmark the pages that matter for a prior-authorisation submission, and mark the item ready. We want an agent to pick it up from there and answer the payer's clinical questions in writing, working from what they bookmarked. The specialist still reviews and submits it.

A nurse reviewer flags the handful of chart pages relevant to a prior-auth request and marks it ready. We would like something to then draft the written answers to the payer's clinical questions off those pages. Nothing goes out without the nurse reading it first.

When an instrument run fails, the technician attaches the vendor's diagnostic dump to the ticket — a few pages of text and tables, laid out differently by every manufacturer. We want an agent to read it and tell the technician in plain language what the instrument was complaining about, so they can decide between recalibrating and calling the vendor. Maybe half a dozen a day.

Five or six times a day an analyser throws an error and dumps a diagnostic file into the ticket. Every manufacturer formats theirs differently. The technician has to skim it to work out whether this is a recalibration or a service call. We would like that skim done for them, in a sentence or two.

Small-grant applications arrive with one or two attachments — usually a budget sheet, sometimes a letter of support. Before a panel member spends an hour on one, we want an agent to look at what came in and say whether there is enough there to assess, recommending proceed, return to the applicant, or hand to a person. The panel still decides.

Panel members are spending time on grant applications that were never going to be assessable. Each application has a couple of attachments. Could something look at them first and tell us: assessable, send back to the applicant, or needs a human to decide? The panel still makes the call.

Quote requests arrive in a shared mailbox, around a hundred thousand a year across eight countries. The request details might be in the email body, in one attachment, or spread across several where only one is the actual request and the rest are supporting material. A good number of the messages are not quote requests at all. Before anything can be captured we have to decide, per message, whether this is a request and which part of it carries it.

One mailbox takes roughly a hundred thousand messages a year from eight countries. Some are quote requests, plenty are not. When one is, the detail might be in the email itself, in an attached PDF or spreadsheet, or in one of several attachments where the others are just background. Our team opens each one to find out which.

Complaints reach us through twelve channels — email, web forms, a legacy messaging system, physical mail — and every one of them has to be sorted into one of seventy-seven categories before a case is opened. Getting the category wrong sends the complaint to the wrong team and restarts the clock. We need the category decided and the case routed; the case record itself gets built afterwards.

Complaints come in by email, web form, an old messaging platform and physical post — twelve routes in total. Each has to land in one of seventy-seven buckets so the right team picks it up. Put it in the wrong bucket and the clock restarts somewhere else. Opening the case record itself is a later step.

For each flagged patient account we read the payer correspondence sitting in our imaging system and decide whether it is a genuine denial, and if so which denial reason applies. Calling a denial when there is not one sends the account down an appeals path that costs weeks. On a blind set we found that pushing critical errors to zero left only about a fifth of volume running untouched, while a looser threshold ran most of it and let real errors through.

Our imaging system holds the payer correspondence for every flagged account. Someone reads it and decides: is this actually a denial, and if it is, which reason code. Say denial when it is not and the account goes into an appeals queue for weeks. We tested it and found that being strict enough to stop those errors left most of the volume still going to people.

Enhanced due diligence on a single institutional client currently takes an analyst around thirty hours and we run about a thousand a year. The analyst works through a defined bundle — corporate registry filings, adverse media, prior reviews, transaction narratives — and produces one written assessment where every statement has to be traceable to the document behind it, including where two sources disagree. Turnaround matters less than the assessment holding up when it is challenged.

Enhanced due diligence on one institutional client runs to about thirty analyst-hours and we do a thousand a year. The analyst reads a known bundle — registry filings, adverse media, previous reviews, transaction narratives — and writes one assessment. It gets challenged, so every line in it has to point back at a source, including where the sources disagree with each other.

Before a regulator inspects a trial site, a quality manager works through that trial's document set and writes a readiness assessment — what is in order, what is missing, what would not survive a question. Every statement has to point at the document behind it, and when the assessment says a requirement is met, that has to be something we can defend.

A quality manager preparing a trial site for inspection reads through that trial's documents and writes up where we stand: in order, missing, or wouldn't hold up if questioned. The write-up cites the document behind each point, and if it says a requirement is satisfied we need to be able to stand behind that.

After a major outage we collect everything: the paging timeline, chat transcripts, change records, vendor status pages, and the on-call engineers' own notes. Someone has to turn that fixed pile into one written post-incident report with a defensible sequence of events, calling out where two sources contradict each other and citing which record supports each claim. The collection is already done and somebody else signs the report off.

After a big outage we end up with a pile of material — pager timeline, the incident channel, change records, vendor status history, engineers' notes. One person then writes the post-incident review off that pile: what happened in what order, citing which record says so, and calling out where two of them tell different stories. Someone else signs it.

Our operations teams keep asking the same kinds of questions about internal standard operating procedures — which approval a given transaction needs, what the cut-off is, which form applies. The SOP library is maintained centrally and reused by everyone; a typical question is settled by one procedure. Live transaction status comes from the operational system, not from the SOPs.

Operations keep asking the back office the same procedural questions — which approval this transaction needs, what time the cut-off is, which form applies. It is all written down in the SOP library that we maintain centrally, and normally one procedure answers it. Where something stands right now still comes from the operational system.

Underwriters need to look up what our own underwriting manual says about a specific risk class. The manual is versioned, the current edition is the one indexed, and the answer is normally a single section they then apply themselves. They want the passage and its edition, not a recommendation — and if the manual genuinely does not address the risk they need to be told that rather than handed the nearest paragraph.

An underwriter looking at an unusual risk wants to know what our manual says about that class. We publish a new edition periodically and the current one is the one that counts. They want the wording and which edition it came from, then they apply it themselves. If the manual is silent on it, they need to hear that.

Our tariff documentation is maintained separately per operating region, and the same term — say, a demurrage free period — means different things region to region. An agent has to answer a definition or procedure question inside one named region and cite the regional document it came from, without blending in another region's wording.

Each operating region maintains its own tariff documentation, and terms like the demurrage free period do not mean the same thing from one to the next. Someone asking about a term will name the region. They need that region's definition and the document it sits in.

Supplier invoices from around two thousand suppliers across five countries arrive in widely varying formats, and we need the same thirty-odd fields off every one of them to post into the finance system. Low-confidence fields have to go to a validation step before anything posts, and a wrong value that gets through becomes a payment error, so per-field accuracy and the correction workflow are both hard requirements.

Two thousand suppliers across five countries send invoices in whatever format they like. We need the same thirty-odd pieces of information off every one to post it into finance. Anything the system is not sure about goes to a person to confirm before it posts — a wrong figure that slips through becomes a payment we have to claw back.

On a death notification we pull the beneficiary details off the policy documentation and cross-check the beneficiary change request against the confirmation letter that acknowledged it. The documents are already sorted by type before we get to them. A wrong beneficiary is the worst outcome we have, so every field goes through validation before a payment is set up, and an unreadable value has to stay unresolved rather than be filled in.

On a death notification we take the beneficiary information off the policy paperwork and check the change request against the letter that confirmed it. Someone has already sorted the documents by type. Paying the wrong beneficiary is the worst thing we can do, so every value is confirmed by a person before a payment is set up, and anything illegible stays blank.

Before a clinician can be placed we verify around seventy-eight requirement types off ten document types — licences, certifications, screening results — running to tens of thousands of checks a month. Each document type has its own fixed field set, the documents are already separated by type, and a missed expiry date places someone who should not be working, so per-field review is mandatory.

Placing a clinician means checking around seventy-eight requirements against ten kinds of document — licences, certifications, screening results. That is tens of thousands of checks a month. Each document type has its own set of things we need off it, they arrive already sorted, and missing an expiry date puts someone on a ward who should not be there.

About a hundred thousand trade-deduction claims a year land as rows in a table, each carrying a short free-text reason a customer's clerk typed — shorthand, abbreviations, sometimes just a promotion name. We want a normalised reason code on every row, from a list we already maintain, so the claims can be matched against agreements later on.

Trade-deduction claims reach us as a file, roughly a hundred thousand a year. Each line has a short note somebody at the customer typed to explain the deduction — abbreviations, internal shorthand, occasionally just a promotion name. We want a code from our standard reason list against each line so they can be reconciled to agreements afterwards.

We pull a month of closed support tickets into a file — tens of thousands of rows — and want two things added to each: a root-cause category from our standard list of about thirty, and a one-line plain-English summary of what went wrong. The only place that information exists is the free-text description the engineer wrote. The file then goes to reporting.

Reporting wants a monthly file of closed tickets with two extra columns filled in: which of our thirty root-cause categories it was, and a one-liner saying what actually went wrong. Tens of thousands of rows. The only source for either is whatever the engineer typed in the description field.

Our product feed has thousands of rows where the attribute columns — material, fit, intended use — are empty, even though the seller's own description usually says. We want those columns filled from that description text using the controlled vocabulary we already publish, and left empty where the description genuinely does not say.

Thousands of products in our feed have blank attribute columns — material, fit, what it is for — while the seller's description says it plainly. We want those columns populated from the description, using the vocabulary we already publish, and left blank where the description does not actually say.
